body:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Polaris Analytics - Dedicated POC scoping (autoscaling bounds + ramp latency)
Date: 2025-06-18
Time: 4:00pm - 4:53pm PT
Duration: 53 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Vanessa Ortiz, Chloe Martin, Lauren Bishop
Polaris Analytics: Sarah Chen, Mark Feldman, Priya Desai

---

Summary (auto-generated)
- Polaris wants a Dedicated POC focused on predictable performance during a daily traffic ramp and strict spend controls.
- Key success criteria: enforce a hard max autoscaling bound and maintain p95 latency during the ramp window.
- Redwood reviewed how Dedicated scaling works today, the upcoming min/max bounds controls, and how predictive signals can pre-scale before the ramp.
- Agreed on pilot enablement steps, metrics, and data needed to size initial min/max values.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Current workload + ramp pattern
2) Dedicated deployment shape and isolation
3) Autoscaling bounds (min/max) semantics
4) p95 latency measurement + what “during ramp” means
5) Pilot logistics and timeline

Questions (auto-generated)
- What happens if we hit the max bound and demand keeps increasing?
- Can Redwood guarantee we never exceed the max even if latency degrades?
- How do we avoid oscillation when predictions are wrong?

---

Transcript

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the Polaris Dedicated POC scoping. Goal today is to nail success criteria, the environment, and what we need from you to kick off. Um, quick intros? I’m Liam, I’m the TAM on Redwood side, I’ll be your day-to-day for the pilot.

[00:16] Sarah Chen: Hey, I’m Sarah, VP Eng. Mark and Priya are on too.

[00:20] Mark Feldman: Mark, I run ML platform here.

[00:22] Priya Desai: Priya, finance ops. I’m mostly here for the “don’t surprise us with bills” part.

[00:27] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. On our side, Vanessa leads fleet autoscaling, Chloe is Console/backend, and Lauren is PM for Dedicated.

[00:36] Lauren Bishop: Hi everyone.

[00:37] Vanessa Ortiz: Hey.

[00:39] Chloe Martin: Hi.

[00:41] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. Sarah, do you want to restate the POC goal in your words? Just so we align.

[00:48] Sarah Chen: Sure. We’re moving an internal assistant feature into production. We’re currently on a mix of hosted APIs and some self-managed stuff. The pain is, we get a daily ramp like… it’s very predictable. 8:30am to 10am our time. And our p95 blows up and people complain.

[01:05] Sarah Chen: But also, we’ve had issues where autoscaling—like on Kubernetes HPA or managed endpoints—scales too aggressively and then we’re paying for peak all day. So we want two things: one, hold a max. Like, a hard ceiling. Two, meet a p95 latency target during that ramp.

[01:23] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. Priya, when you say hard ceiling, is it “never exceed X GPUs” or “never exceed X dollars”?

[01:31] Priya Desai: Ideally both, but I’ll take a capacity cap as a proxy. Like, if we agree it’s, I don’t know, 16 GPUs, I want to be sure we don’t go to 24 because some signal freaked out.

[01:44] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s exactly what min/max bounds are meant to do. Like literally clamp the desired replica count. Even if the reactive signal says “go up,” you hit the max and you stay there.

[01:56] Mark Feldman: But then doesn’t latency just get worse? Like if you clamp it, you’re admitting it might degrade.

[02:03] Vanessa Ortiz: Correct. The ceiling is a spend guardrail. It trades off performance when you’re beyond that capacity. That’s why we recommend having a min baseline and a max ceiling that’s actually enough for your peak, if you truly need that p95 target.

[02:16] Sarah Chen: For the POC, we want to prove the controls work and we can choose the right bounds.

[02:21] Liam O'Rourke: That makes sense. Mark, can you describe the workload a bit? Model size, context lengths, concurrency.

[02:29] Mark Feldman: Yeah. Mostly chat completions. Context length is… kind of bimodal. A lot of short stuff, but we also have long threads. Maybe 2k tokens typical, but sometimes 10k.

[02:41] Mark Feldman: Concurrency during ramp is like 3x normal. Normal is 40 requests per second, ramp peak maybe 120 RPS. Output tokens average 250-ish but can spike.

[02:53] Chloe Martin: And are you doing streaming? Or do you wait for full response.

[02:57] Mark Feldman: Streaming for the UI, yeah.

[03:00] Chloe Martin: Ok. That matters for p95 measurement—we’ll want to define whether we measure time-to-first-token or full completion.

[03:07] Sarah Chen: For us, user experience is time to first token. But we also look at completion sometimes.

[03:13] Lauren Bishop: We can set success criteria on both, but commonly we do TTFT p95 and then a throughput or tokens/sec metric.

[03:22] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s park metrics for a second. Vanessa, can you explain how scaling works today in Dedicated and what changes in this feature?

[03:29] Vanessa Ortiz: Sure. Today, the autoscaler looks at saturation signals—GPU utilization-ish, queue depth, and request latency. It computes a desired replica count. Operators can override, but there isn’t a customer-facing “hard min/hard max” with deterministic rules.

[03:47] Vanessa Ortiz: What we’re shipping—what you’re asking for—is a per-deployment policy: min replicas, max replicas, cooldowns. And optional predictive mode where we take forecasted demand and bias scale-up earlier, so you don’t build a queue before scaling.

[04:04] Priya Desai: When you say “bias”, does that mean it can exceed max?

[04:09] Vanessa Ortiz: No. Max is hard. Predictive is only part of “requested desired.” Then we apply bounds. So the bounded desired can never exceed max and never go below min.

[04:22] Sarah Chen: That’s a key requirement.

[04:24] Liam O'Rourke: Same for us. We also emit metrics that show “requested desired vs bounded desired” so it’s auditable.

[04:33] Mark Feldman: What about if the prediction is wrong? Like it thinks we’ll ramp and we don’t.

[04:40] Vanessa Ortiz: Then you might temporarily run hotter than needed, but we have safeguards: cooldowns, anti-oscillation, and we still use reactive signals. If reactive says “there’s no load,” we’ll scale down but not below min and not too aggressively.

[04:55] Lauren Bishop: And for pilot we can keep predictive as optional. You can start with reactive + bounds only, then turn predictive on once we have a baseline.

[05:05] Sarah Chen: I’d like that. Priya probably prefers that.

[05:08] Priya Desai: Yes. One variable at a time please.

[05:11] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Now, success criteria. I heard two: (1) max bound enforced, (2) p95 latency during ramp. Let’s make them measurable.

[05:22] Chloe Martin: Also we should include something like “no surprise scale to zero” or “no dropping below baseline.” We’ve seen weirdness in other systems.

[05:28] Sarah Chen: Agree. Minimum baseline matters because cold start is what kills us.

[05:34] Vanessa Ortiz: Then we should set a min bound. Like if your baseline needed is, say, 6 replicas, we’ll keep at least 6.

[05:41] Mark Feldman: Replica equals GPU?

[05:44] Vanessa Ortiz: In Dedicated, depending on the model profile, one replica maps to a GPU slice or a full GPU. For this POC, we’ll likely do 1 replica = 1 GPU worker, to keep it simple. We’ll confirm based on model.

[05:58] Mark Feldman: Ok.

[06:00] Liam O'Rourke: On p95: Sarah you said TTFT p95. Do you have a target number?

[06:06] Sarah Chen: If we can keep time to first token under 800ms p95 during ramp, that’s a win. Today it goes to like 2-3 seconds. Completion p95 can be higher, like 10-12 seconds, but we mostly care about responsiveness.

[06:23] Lauren Bishop: 800ms p95 TTFT is aggressive but doable depending on context length. We’ll want to stratify by prompt size. If you have a bunch of 10k prompts, TTFT might be different.

[06:35] Sarah Chen: Totally. We can define it for the “standard” route. Most are <4k.

[06:40] Chloe Martin: Great. So success metric could be “TTFT p95 < 800ms for requests with prompt_tokens <= 4096 during the ramp window.”

[06:51] Mark Feldman: That sounds reasonable.

[06:53] Liam O'Rourke: And define ramp window. You said 8:30 to 10am your time. What timezone?

[06:59] Sarah Chen: Eastern.

[07:00] Liam O'Rourke: Ok, so 5:30 to 7:00 PT. Our infra is in us-west for pilot unless you need east.

[07:08] Sarah Chen: West is fine for now. Production might be multi region later but not for this.

[07:14] Vanessa Ortiz: That also matters because predictive mode can get timezone wrong if it’s not explicit. We’ve had… issues. So we’ll be explicit.

[07:24] Mark Feldman: Sorry, did you say you’ve had issues already?

[07:27] Vanessa Ortiz: Not with you—just in general, when forecast inputs are UTC and people think local time. We’ve learned to be explicit.

[07:35] Liam O'Rourke: For the POC we’ll document: ramp window is defined in customer local timezone, we store it with timezone.

[07:44] Priya Desai: Ok.

[07:46] Liam O'Rourke: Now on the max bound. Priya, what number would make you comfortable? Or do we size based on budget.

[07:54] Priya Desai: We have an internal ceiling for this feature. I can share after the call. Roughly, we don’t want to exceed what would be like, say, 20k a month for inference. But I know it depends on usage.

[08:07] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah, for the pilot we can translate that to max GPU count with an assumption of utilization. But the simplest is: we agree on max replicas for pilot. We can iterate.

[08:20] Sarah Chen: I’d rather pick a max that’s enough to meet the p95 goal. If we pick too low, we’ll just prove it’s clamped but performance will fail.

[08:29] Priya Desai: I mean yes, but I need confidence we won’t blow it up.

[08:33] Lauren Bishop: For POC, we can do two scenarios: A) max bound set intentionally low to show enforcement and how it surfaces, and B) max bound sized to meet the ramp. That way you validate both spend guardrail and performance.

[08:47] Mark Feldman: That’s smart. We can run a controlled load test.

[08:51] Vanessa Ortiz: And we’ll have a dashboard panel that literally shows “bounded by max” events. Like a counter and a timeline.

[09:01] Chloe Martin: Plus the Console will show “You are at max capacity” state for that deployment.

[09:07] Sarah Chen: In terms of how it surfaces, can you also alert? Like if we’re hitting max and queue depth is rising.

[09:14] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. For pilot we can set alerting to your on-call email or Slack via webhook. Internally we also page our SRE if it’s sustained.

[09:23] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll coordinate that. Ok. Let’s talk about what you need to run the POC. Mark, do you have a load testing harness already?

[09:31] Mark Feldman: We do. K6 plus some custom token accounting. But we’ll need your SDK endpoints.

[09:37] Chloe Martin: We can provide a sample script. Also we need to make sure we’re measuring TTFT correctly with streaming. Sometimes K6 just measures full response.

[09:47] Mark Feldman: Yeah, we have a workaround. We parse the first chunk.

[09:52] Liam O'Rourke: Great. On our side, we’ll stand up a Dedicated deployment in us-west, with a single model route matching your target model. Which model are you thinking? You mentioned open models earlier.

[10:04] Mark Feldman: We’re considering Llama 3.1 70B, but maybe too big. We might do 8B for the assistant. We’re still deciding.

[10:13] Vanessa Ortiz: For 70B, the capacity math is very different. For ramp p95 TTFT, 8B or 13B is much easier. If your app can tolerate it quality-wise, it’ll save you money too.

[10:24] Sarah Chen: We can start with the smaller one for POC. The product team is ok with that.

[10:30] Lauren Bishop: If you want, we can run an eval set later. For now, focus on serving behavior.

[10:37] Priya Desai: Yes please, focus on serving.

[10:40] Liam O'Rourke: Ok. Autoscaling policy: We’ll set min and max. You said baseline matters. Do you know your baseline capacity today?

[10:49] Mark Feldman: On our self-managed cluster, we keep 4 A10s warm. During ramp we go to 10.

[10:57] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s helpful. Not apples-to-apples but gives a starting point. In Dedicated we might start min=4, max=12, then adjust.

[11:06] Sarah Chen: And the test scenario is the daily ramp. We can replay it.

[11:11] Liam O'Rourke: Yep. We’ll likely ask for a 7-day traffic histogram: requests per minute, prompt tokens, output tokens. Doesn’t need to include content, just counts.

[11:23] Mark Feldman: We can do that.

[11:25] Priya Desai: Please tell me no PII needed.

[11:28] Liam O'Rourke: No PII. Just aggregate metrics.

[11:32] Sarah Chen: Good.

[11:34] Chloe Martin: On the bounds config: in pilot we can set it in Console or via API. Do you prefer IaC? Terraform.

[11:41] Mark Feldman: For POC, Console is fine. Long-term we’ll want Terraform.

[11:46] Chloe Martin: Ok. For the pilot we’ll use Console, and we can share the API payload so you can automate later.

[11:54] Sarah Chen: So the actual success criteria doc should say what is enabled. Like, “bounds feature flag” right?

[12:02] Lauren Bishop: Correct. This is behind a feature flag per account/deployment. We’ll enable it for Polaris’ pilot deployment only.

[12:11] Liam O'Rourke: I’ll open the internal request once we have the deployment ID.

[12:16] Mark Feldman: Is there any risk of it changing behavior unexpectedly?

[12:21] Vanessa Ortiz: It shouldn’t change behavior unless you set the fields. Defaults preserve existing behavior. But for the pilot we’ll explicitly set them so it’s deterministic.

[12:32] Sarah Chen: Can we talk about what happens when max is hit? Like do requests fail or queue.

[12:37] Vanessa Ortiz: Neither immediately. If max is hit and demand keeps rising, you’ll see queue depth increase and latency increase. We can configure admission control if you want to fail fast after some threshold.

[12:50] Sarah Chen: We probably want fail-fast for the UI rather than 30 second hangs.

[12:55] Mark Feldman: Yeah, we’d rather return a friendly “busy” response.

[12:59] Vanessa Ortiz: We can discuss SLO policy: max queue time or max concurrent. It’s separate from bounds but interacts.

[13:09] Lauren Bishop: For POC scope, we can keep it simple: observe what happens at max and ensure it’s visible and alerts. Fail-fast tuning can be phase 2.

[13:20] Sarah Chen: Ok.

[13:22] Liam O'Rourke: On predictive scaling—do we want it in POC or not.

[13:26] Priya Desai: Not initially.

[13:28] Mark Feldman: I’m interested, but fine to postpone.

[13:31] Vanessa Ortiz: We can still design the test so it’s easy to turn on later. Like you run the same ramp scenario twice: reactive only, and reactive+predictive, compare queue buildup at ramp start.

[13:44] Sarah Chen: That’s compelling. Maybe we add it as optional stretch goal.

[13:48] Liam O'Rourke: Great. So baseline POC success is bounds + latency. Stretch goal: predictive reduces ramp pain.

[13:57] Chloe Martin: Also, audit logs. Some customers ask “who changed the bounds.” Do you care?

[14:03] Sarah Chen: For us, eventually yes. Not a blocker for POC.

[14:07] Priya Desai: I care. We’ve had incidents where someone changed a setting and no one knew.

[14:12] Lauren Bishop: Our plan is to emit audit events for scaling policy changes and scaling decisions. For pilot, we can provide the event logs on request, and we’ll have retention internally.

[14:25] Priya Desai: Ok.

[14:27] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk timeline. If you can send traffic aggregates by end of week, we can stand up the deployment early next week and run initial load test mid-week.

[14:39] Sarah Chen: That works.

[14:40] Mark Feldman: We have a product checkpoint next Friday. If we can show progress, good.

[14:45] Liam O'Rourke: Great. A couple more detailed questions: Are you single tenant per environment? Any data residency.

[14:52] Sarah Chen: For this assistant, data is mostly internal but not regulated like HIPAA. US-only is fine.

[14:59] Liam O'Rourke: Ok. Dedicated in us-west meets that.

[15:02] Mark Feldman: One thing: we have spiky bursts on top of the ramp. Like a cron job kicks off.

[15:08] Vanessa Ortiz: Is it scheduled?

[15:10] Mark Feldman: Pretty much. 9:05am every day.

[15:13] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s exactly where predictive is useful. But also we can do step scaling: pre-scale at 9:00. But that’s manual scheduling. Predictive automates it.

[15:24] Sarah Chen: We can share that schedule.

[15:27] Chloe Martin: If it’s a scheduled event, we could also accept “scheduled minimum” as an input. Not sure if it’s in current scope.

[15:34] Lauren Bishop: Not in initial scope, but it’s close to the predictive idea. For pilot, we can treat it as a known event and watch if reactive handles it.

[15:45] Liam O'Rourke: Ok. Priya, any requirements on reporting? Like you need a weekly cost breakdown.

[15:51] Priya Desai: Yes. I want to know tokens, GPU hours, whatever you have. And I want to see if hitting max happened.

[15:59] Chloe Martin: Console has token-level cost and latency breakdown. For Dedicated it shows compute hours and request metrics per route. And we’ll have “bound hit rate.”

[16:10] Priya Desai: Great.

[16:12] Mark Feldman: On the latency target: you said it depends on prompt length. For our ramp, do you want us to filter out the long prompts?

[16:19] Vanessa Ortiz: We should include them, but you can segment. Like p95 for <=4k, and separately for >4k. Otherwise the numbers get confusing.

[16:29] Sarah Chen: That’s fine.

[16:31] Liam O'Rourke: Also, what’s your current p95 baseline when not ramping?

[16:36] Mark Feldman: Around 400-500ms TTFT.

[16:39] Liam O'Rourke: Great. So target during ramp is <800ms. That’s a reasonable “no more than 2x degrade” type target.

[16:48] Sarah Chen: Exactly.

[16:50] Liam O'Rourke: Ok. Can we talk about failure mode when min cannot be met? Like if the region is out of GPUs.

[16:58] Sarah Chen: That would be bad.

[17:00] Vanessa Ortiz: In Dedicated, we reserve capacity, so if we contractually reserve N, we should be able to meet min. For pilot it’s best effort but we’ll choose a region where we have headroom. If we cannot meet min, we surface a degraded state and alert.

[17:18] Priya Desai: Does that mean you might still charge us for min even if not met?

[17:22] Liam O'Rourke: For pilot, we’ll keep billing simple; we’ll discuss commercial later. For GA Dedicated contracts, min is tied to reserved capacity so it’s guaranteed.

[17:34] Priya Desai: Ok.

[17:36] Chloe Martin: Quick UI question: when you set min and max, do you want “recommended range” guidance? Or you decide.

[17:42] Sarah Chen: Guidance would help. But for POC, we’ll work with you.

[17:48] Vanessa Ortiz: We’ll propose a starting point, then iterate based on data.

[17:52] Liam O'Rourke: Cool.

[18:00] (Crosstalk)

[18:01] Mark Feldman: Sorry, one more—do you do continuous batching? We’ve seen queue depth get weird when batching changes.

[18:08] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, we do continuous batching and KV cache optimizations. And you’re right: queue depth is not always a stable metric depending on batching. That’s why our autoscaler uses multiple signals, not just queue.

[18:22] Mark Feldman: Ok. As long as it doesn’t oscillate.

[18:25] Vanessa Ortiz: We have anti-oscillation guardrails: cooldowns and dampening. Also we can set minimum step sizes.

[18:33] Sarah Chen: Oscillation is one of my fears, especially if we later turn predictive on.

[18:39] Lauren Bishop: That’s why we’re rolling it out with feature flags and canary. For your POC, bounds-only should be stable.

[18:48] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Let’s lock success criteria:

[18:52] Liam O'Rourke: 1) Max bound: When configured to max=X, the deployment never exceeds X replicas/GPU workers. Evidence: metrics and audit trail showing bounded_desired <= X at all times.

[19:05] Liam O'Rourke: 2) Baseline min: When configured min=Y, we never scale below Y, and cold start during ramp is avoided.

[19:14] Liam O'Rourke: 3) Performance: During the defined ramp window (8:30-10:00 ET), TTFT p95 < 800ms for prompt_tokens<=4096, measured at client side or via Redwood metrics (we’ll align).

[19:31] Liam O'Rourke: 4) Observability: Polaris can view desired vs bounded replicas, bound-hit events, queue depth/latency graphs in Console; and alerts for sustained max-bound saturation + queue growth.

[19:44] Sarah Chen: That sounds good.

[19:46] Priya Desai: Add cost visibility too. Like I can see the spend in the pilot.

[19:50] Liam O'Rourke: Yep. Add 5) Cost reporting available daily: tokens and compute hours.

[19:58] Chloe Martin: Works.

[20:00] Mark Feldman: How do we run the “max intentionally low” scenario? We don’t want to break the UI.

[20:06] Vanessa Ortiz: We can do it in a load test environment, not your production traffic. You replay the ramp and set max low; we confirm bounded behavior and alerting. Then set max to a better value and re-run.

[20:20] Mark Feldman: Perfect.

[20:22] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Pilot enablement: We’ll need to enable the feature flag. That requires internal approval but it’s straightforward. Lauren, is Polaris on the pilot list?

[20:31] Lauren Bishop: They’re a good candidate, yes. We’ll do it per deployment.

[20:37] Liam O'Rourke: Ok.

[20:39] Sarah Chen: What do you need from us besides traffic data?

[20:42] Liam O'Rourke: Model choice (8B vs 70B), token distribution, and your test harness details. Also confirm if you need VPC peering or just public endpoint with IP allowlist.

[20:54] Sarah Chen: For POC, public with allowlist is fine.

[20:57] Mark Feldman: We can give you our egress IPs.

[21:00] Chloe Martin: Great.

[21:02] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else? Priya, any procurement hurdles for a POC.

[21:07] Priya Desai: Not for a pilot if it’s within credits. If it turns into contract, we’ll loop legal.

[21:14] Liam O'Rourke: Ok.

[21:16] (brief pause)

[21:18] Sarah Chen: One concern. If we’re relying on min capacity, but the platform can’t provision, how will we know quickly.

[21:25] Vanessa Ortiz: We will show a “min unmet” degraded state and alert. It’s rare in Dedicated because capacity is reserved, but for pilot it’s possible if we pick an over-subscribed instance type. We’ll choose something with headroom.

[21:39] Sarah Chen: Ok.

[21:42] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, let’s do recap and next steps.

[21:46] Liam O'Rourke: Next steps:
- Polaris (Mark/Sarah) sends 7-day traffic aggregates and ramp schedule with timezone; also egress IPs.
- Redwood (Vanessa) proposes initial min/max + cooldown.
- Redwood (Chloe) confirms Console/API steps to set the policy.
- Redwood (Liam) sends POC plan doc + opens internal ticket for feature flag enablement once deployment is created.

[22:10] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll schedule a technical working session early next week to review the load test plan and how we measure TTFT.

[22:19] Sarah Chen: Sounds good.

[22:20] Mark Feldman: Yep.

[22:21] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[22:23] Liam O'Rourke: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by email.

(Transcript ends; remainder of the call had minor off-topic scheduling chatter.)
